articles.summary: It is not every day that a company can settle a case for over $17 billion and celebrate. However, Meta’s proposed settlement of claims brought by a coalition originally led by 29 states on Wednesday is a remarkably good deal for a company facing potential penalties that Meta estimated could reach $1.4 trillion and years of litigation. In the end, the company may not even take a loss from the litigation. The proposed settlement ends the states’ federal case (but not the wider wave of litigation), following similar settlements in tobacco, opiates and other products. It will require Meta to make changes to its platform, though the company has already appeared to be moving to make such changes. articles.summary: As a performer, Tim Curry knew how to walk a fine line. Even his most sinister characters had an ironic sort of appeal, because watching Curry have fun is, in itself, fun. The actor, who died yesterday at age 80, acted with palpable glee: He could produce a real-life version of the Grinch’s ever-widening grin and could commit to sheer silliness in a way that freed him to twirl around in a cape while singing a gibberish song about Halloween . Perhaps nowhere was this more evident than in the 1985 film Clue . When the raucous comedy adaptation of the classic whodunit board game debuted in theaters, Paramount Pictures had a unique plan: Instead of one ending, the movie would have three, and audiences never knew which resolution—which killer, in which room, with which weapon—they were going to see. How could the studio sell viewers on a story as convoluted as Clue , whose script was designed to keep people guessing until the very last second? By recruiting an ensemble of comedy greats led by Curry, of course. The actor could easily inhabit a character who was neither wholly a hero nor totally a villain, but rather a merrily odd mix of both. [ Read: The absolute pleasure of Tim Curry ]

articles.summary: My introduction to Dolly Parton came at 7. My mom, as the lead alto in the church choir, had some sway with our music director and she used it to snag me the occasional solo in front of the congregation. I sang hymns, some contemporary Christian songs. Then one day, Mom brought home the sheet music for “Coat of Many Colors.” The song wasn’t in the Baptist hymnal, but she seemed confident it would pass muster (after all, who doesn’t love Dolly?). I practiced at home, committing the lyrics to heart. I took my position on stage by the pulpit one Sunday, facing pews stuffed with people, and scanned the crowd for my mom as I started to sing. For the first time during one of my performances, she wept. My mom drew the parallels between Parton’s song and her own life — she, too, had grown up as an impoverished kid from a big family, and she’d learned a little bit about turning humble beginnings into something greater. That’s what brought her to tears, not my tinny soprano. That day I realized how music — how storytelling — can move people. And over the course of her seven-decade career, Dolly Parton moved many .
